utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before we begin, Mr. Kehoe, and before we bring in Witness R in a few moments, a few moments before this hearing we spoke about changing the schedule somewhat with Mr. Harmon. So that my colleagues will be informed, Mr. Harmon might be able to inform us about how the rest of the week looks. I think things got a little bit changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning counsel. Thank you. Mr. President, we have had some witnesses who have not been able to appear as initially intended. In order to fill the gap we have asked additional witnesses to arrive from Bosnia. They will be arriving this evening, late, and because of the lateness of the hour we will be only presenting one of those witnesses Thursday, and another witness we have is not available until Friday morning, he will be testifying on Friday morning and then we will carry over the witness who is the second Bosnian witness, who will be arriving tomorrow night, we will carry him over until Monday of the following week. So after today's witnesses, we will be presenting Thursday and Friday two witnesses, one on each day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In order to summarise, we have this morning's witness, and how many witnesses will we have today, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have three additional witnesses after this morning's witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am sorry, maybe I did not wake up right. You are saying for today's witnesses, we have the end of Witness R's testimony and then for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have three additional witnesses, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And for tomorrow you have one, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, in the afternoon, all right. Therefore today and tomorrow morning, we have three, after Witness R; tomorrow, Thursday in the afternoon, we will have one witness; and Friday morning, one. As you understand, in light of the large amount of work which we are being asked to do, given the Defence motions, we are very busy, just as you are. The judges would like for all of this to be done as quickly as possible, therefore we will begin at 9.00 on Friday, but will not meet in the afternoon, so that if we begin at 9.00 and end at 1.00, but we will be finished at the end of Friday morning. For next week, I would like to remind you we will conclude our hearings on Wednesday evening and as much as possible, all the witnesses should be heard, as my colleagues have recalled, so that we can avoid having to break the testimonies and move them into January. You know that the schedule for the Blaskic trial is very, very complicated because other trials must be taken into consideration as well. We are beginning to have a clearer understanding what is going to happen, there were some changes that were made. I would like to be cautious and make final announcements about the schedule only next week. Having settled these issues, I think we can now bring in the witness, unless there are any other comments anybody wishes to make. We can now therefore continue with the examination. No comments from the Defence? Thank you. I would like to remind you that this is an open hearing, I am saying this for the public gallery, but we have drawn the blinds so that the witness can come in, but after he does, we will be in public, unless there are certain points in his testimony which have to be kept private. That is how we continue to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, on a separate issue for the next witness, the next witness is Sergeant Ian Parrott, again of the Cheshire Regiment. He will not need the protective measures taken for this witness and other witnesses. However, we will need to set up the easel again as we have done with previous witnesses, so if the court can bear with us for just a couple of minutes while we set this stuff up, after Witness R is finished, I would appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We always show indulgence. The witness is now coming in. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness R, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You feel good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Then you will continue to answer the questions that the Prosecutor is going to ask. We can now continue. WITNESS R (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning Witness R. If I may, with the assistance of Mr. Dubuisson, have Exhibit 166 brought out, and the maps, which were 161, 162 and 163, if we could bring those back in and I would like to focus at this juncture on the map 163. Witness R, we left off yesterday speaking about the events concerning Exhibit 163 and the various locations in 163 and the location on this map that is marked 24 was where you previously testified that you and other refugees from Donje Veceriska were taken to the UNPROFOR location, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did this group of individuals in and about the UNPROFOR station, did they include women, children, old people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all women, children and elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a series of photographs, and I believe we are at 166/2, we have talked about 166/1 already. The next three photographs, Mr. President and your Honours, are photographs of what has been known and called the echelon garage, it is the UNPROFOR station, and these were taken by British Cheshire Regiment soldiers. The first photograph, Witness R, is this the group of individuals -- a part of the group of people that were out in front of the echelon starting on 18th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do they include in that photograph women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can see on the photograph very well that they are all women and children and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you point to that, Witness R, point to the women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you can see the women and children and behind (indicates), below this structure. This was later covered with nylon and that is where the women and children were. We called it the tent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So are the soldiers in the process of erecting that tent as this photograph is taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were just erecting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next photograph, Witness R, which is just a different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us try and go a little more quickly, Mr. Kehoe, and not get back into old bad habits. We can see that there are women and children here, they can also make the distinction between civilians and military personnel. Let us not waste time with that, please. I am sorry to say this in front of the witness, but he is not going to tell the judges what they see. He can say what he sees, but we can see what we do. Let us try to go more quickly, please. Let us get to the heart of the testimony. He spoke about the tragedy which took place yesterday. Please ask additional questions which are related to the indictment. We can see there are civilians and military personnel. Let us try to speed up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just moving through that photograph and the next paragraph 166/3, can you put that on the ELMO, sir? I am sorry, I think it is the next photograph. I apologise, 166/4. Again, a similar angle of the same gathering of individuals, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: in Donje Veceriska continued to be burnt and you pointed on the photograph to points 26, 27, 28 and 29.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next photograph, and I believe that is 166/5. Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that photograph, do you see the position that is burning, 26 on the map, the smoke visible on this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you point to it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about the area that you have that is burning, point 27?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is, the thick smoke here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about point 28?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Point 29?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These other photographs, if we could just go through them in series, Mr. Usher. I believe we are now at 166/6, we can go to 166/7, 166/8 and 166/9. All those photographs are various time frames of the houses burning in Donje Veceriska on 18th April 1993, as depicted in 26, 27, 28 and 29, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness R, the area that you picked out as 27 that was burning, was that the area of the mektep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was close to it, but I could not see exactly whether it was the mektaba, but I am sure it was a house on fire, but I cannot be sure whether it was the mektaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But it was certainly in the area of the mektep, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what a mektep is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a religious house of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there any other mosque or a mosque with a minaret, for instance, in Donje Veceriska, or was the mektep the sole Muslim religious gathering place in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the only religious building in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness R, you said these events took place on 18th April. Several days later, you continued to remain in the UNPROFOR station and did you see the HVO troops firing from the SPS factory on to the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everybody could see. The soldiers could see everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could see heavy shelling just near the British battalion, heavy shelling of Gacice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is the area from which you saw the heavy shelling, is that depicted in the map on Exhibit 163?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What number is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that shelling taking place from inside the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said in your testimony that after you had been in the area of the UNPROFOR station for several days and then you were taken to another location with the assistance of UNPROFOR, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the assistance of UNPROFOR and the Red Cross, I was transferred to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to go back to the village of Donje Veceriska since that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to go back and vote on any occasion more recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did go for the voting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are there any Muslims living in Donje Veceriska when you went back there for the voting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not a single Muslim is living in Donje Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may turn to our last series of exhibits, Mr. President, that is Exhibit 164 and Exhibit 165, and we will move through these quickly. Witness R, you assisted the Office of the Prosecutor in preparing the map that is before you with the houses circled and picking out these houses from the series of photographs that are depicted in Exhibit 165, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, you identified those houses in a legend, in a list that is connected to the map, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These photographs depict in part the destruction of the Muslim houses in Donje Veceriska, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go through these relatively quickly, Mr. President, your Honours. The photograph that we have is Exhibit 165/1, which is 371 on the front. Whose house is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is Dzemo Haskic's old house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is this the individual that you said was shot and was bleeding on the morning of the 16th, whose daughter asked you to come and help him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is he living in Donje Veceriska any longer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next photograph. On the map it is B, which is 374 in the corner. Whose house is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the house of Rahima Haskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are they living in Donje Veceriska any longer, that family?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have an objection to make. The witness said that not a single Muslim is living in Donje Veceriska any more, so it is just a waste of time if we go from one name to another to establish they are not living in Donje Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was hesitating to make that remark since the witness is here, I would like him to express -- I would like the witness to be able to express himself as he wants. Could we not move things along quickly? Could he not just take them, he saw them, maybe he could make a quick comment about all the photographs and then tender them into evidence. This is the presiding judge speaking to you. You have all these photos, you have already seen them, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What are these photos, the photos that he showed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These photographs show that more or less all Muslim houses were burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have any comments you would like to make? Go ahead, speak spontaneously. Say that you saw all of these photographs, they are all in the record of the Tribunal, do not be worried, they have been tendered into evidence. General Blaskic's attorneys are not contesting them. Do you have anything to say about all of these photographs? Take your time if you need to, and then we will take them in as evidence. Please express yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From these photographs, we can see that the houses were burnt down, many of them were blown up. I do not know what else I would add, except that they were Muslim houses and it is evident from the photographs that the Croatian houses remained intact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness R. I now turn to the Defence, is there any objection to having these put into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour, subject to a date being established, a date of what these represent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you give us a date for the photographs, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The date these were taken or the date the burning took place? The burning took place on 16th, 17th and 18th and we will have a witness who says the burning was taking place as late as 20th May 1993. These photographs were taken in May 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We will accept they are from May 1996 your Honour and with that representation, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, all right, we will take them into evidence, along with the map. Have you completed your examination, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, your Honour, there are several questions concerning these photographs that I think are pertinent to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You want to ask some more questions about these photos, but they have just been filed. We cannot talk about them any more. The Tribunal considers that it has been informed about them and that is all that has to be said. You have to work a little bit differently, Mr. Kehoe. We cannot take your system completely. The Tribunal has been informed about what these photographs are. The witness has had all the time he needed to express himself about them, they have not been contested by the Defence, therefore I think it would be better to move to another question. This is in the transcript and I take responsibility for it. Move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, pardon me, but the point about this is there are several Muslim houses that were attacked that morning and now Croats are living in Muslim houses. That was the point I was going to address, that Croats are living in houses Muslims were driven out of, and I was going to point to one of those photographs. The Office of the Prosecutor finds that somewhat significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I believe that we are wasting a lot of time. One of my colleagues has made a sign to me, saying that he accepts the objection. I will accept it as well, but I believe we are wasting a lot of time. I say it and I say it again. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The Defence accepts this assertion, that Croats are living in Muslim houses in Donje Veceriska, refugee Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, I keep my decision, I want you to move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next series of photographs I would like to identify for the record will identify the identity of Witness R, so I ask at this point, Mr. President and your Honours, if we can go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, this will now be a private session. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Right, we are now in open court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness R, in conclusion, after 16th April 1993, your parents were killed and you essentially lost everything that you owned as well, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness. I am sorry, I have just been reminded by my colleague, if I have not already, Mr. President, I would ask to introduce into evidence Exhibit 161 through Exhibit 166. I believe there has been a stipulation on Exhibits 164 and 165.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The only objection, your Honour, is to Exhibit 166/1, the photograph of the anti-aircraft gun. We do not object to it as a picture representing a gun that the witness recognised, but Mr. Kehoe attempted to draw a connection with the particular location at which this gun was photographed, and yet there is no date of the photograph. We do not know what year or month it was taken and until that is established, we would object to the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you have to tell us when the photograph was taken, which seems to have been the same time as the events because it was taken by the Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this was provided by a soldier from the Cheshire Regiment. As Witness R identified, the photo takes place across the street from the Hotel Vitez. The photo was taken prior to 16th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We would like to examine a witness on that, your Honour. It is not sufficient for counsel to make a representation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I have to say that -- of course you can do what you want when it is your witness, you can ask any questions that you like, but I believe that the Prosecutor has just answered. We have the person who took it, we have the events, we have the locations, I will go back to this notion which is recognised internationally in law, the Tribunal considers that it is informed. I am sorry to have to say this, but I will say it many times from now on. Now you can ask any questions that you want of the witness, but in principle, it will be tendered into evidence with the clarifications Mr. Kehoe has given. If in your questions, Mr. Hayman, you want further information, this will simply be more information for the judges. You may now move to your cross-examination. Will it be you or Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It will be Mr. Nobilo, your Honour. I would just note, we cannot ask this witness about this photo because he does not know when it was taken or who took it. We can only ask Mr. Kehoe about that, and query if he is being tendered on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We have settled this issue, Mr. Hayman. You can ask the witness any questions you like. The Prosecutor has answered. I repeat that the Tribunal is well enough informed and will accept it as evidence with the identifying elements that were given to it. This incident for the second time is now settled. Mr. Nobilo, move to your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. R. I am Anto Nobilo and together with my colleague Russell Hayman, we represent General Blaskic and we would like to ask you several questions for clarification. We saw aerial shots of Donje Veceriska, but we cannot see everything well. Is Donje Veceriska on a hill above the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little bit higher ground, but it is still part of the plains.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Does it border on the fence of the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The village of Gacice, is it also on the hill and is it also bordering on the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before the conflict, how large was the population of Donje Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number, 200 or 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mean 200 or 300 families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the percentage of the Muslim and Croat population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think 60 to 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Which way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 60 per cent of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say 200 to 300 families, is that 200 to 300 households in Donje Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number, but I think that is about the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did any refugees, refugee Muslims come to your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were from Karaula, from Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is the information correct that there were 29 military conscripts among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Among the Muslims, how many military conscripts were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number, but few, very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You would not agree with the information that I have that there were 121 military conscripts among the Muslims in Donje Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before this conflict, did you have any trenches dug up around your houses in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Muslim soldiers in Donje Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know who it was. I am not sure that one existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you know Memsur Haskic, son of Midhat Haskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was he a commander of some kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you know Sulejman Kalco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was his duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not live in Donje Veceriska at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But did he have any duty in Donje Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he lived in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it correct information that I have that Cazim and Midhat and the rest of the Haskics had a heavy machine-gun, M84, ten automatic rifles, two hunting rifles, ten pistols in their house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The press conference on television that you saw on the eve of the attack, do you know what the subject was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall well, but I know that it was from -- I do not know, it was TV Vitez and TV Busovaca, I do not know which station carried it. But I cannot recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You do not know what it discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the eve of the attack, were you a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Witness R, did you give, on 23rd April 1993, did you give a statement to the security service in Zenica? Let me read it to you: "I was a member of the BH army up until 16th April 1993 when the conflict between the army and the Croats began."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not call this a conflict and I was a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you say this to the state security service in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall having said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, I would like to show the original report of the state security sector in Zenica, signed by Witness R, so that Witness R could confirm whether he had signed it and whether the last sentence, which quotes: "I have nothing else to say, I personally dictated this statement and everything stated therein I confirm to be true and I confirm that with my own signature whether this is true." I would just like him to confirm that this was his signature and that he signed it. This is, by the way, a document received from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is the question I was going to ask. It is a document which comes from the Prosecutor. All right, Mr. Kehoe? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am not certain of the document, but that is the representation of counsel, I believe it. I have a translation in English, I do not have the translation in Bosnian, but I take counsel's word for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Witness R, it is natural for the Defence counsel to present documents, that is part of the cross-examination. All right, Mr. Nobilo, continue. Show it to him. The usher will help you. Did you underline the passages? Is this in English -- passages that were translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is the original in Bosnian or Croat or Serbian language, but I also have a translation. I would like to show the Witness R his own signature on the last page of it. Whether he has signed it -- whether he signed this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will need it in cross-examination later. (Handed). In other words, Mr. R, is it correct that you personally dictated this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I dictated this report but I was, so to say, very upset because of my parents' deaths, so I never read it afterwards but I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you dictated it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now that we have shown you this, do you stay by your claim that you were not a member of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And can you say how it happened that you dictated this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall, because I was not fully aware of everything that happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. In the examination-in-chief, you told the Prosecutor that the relationship between the Muslims and the Croats within the village were good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there not a problem with some wood at the entrance of Donje Veceriska and there were 30 Muslims and Croats who had drawn guns at one another at one point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no objection to counsel getting into this subject matter, but if cross-examination is going to be restricted by direct, this is a subject matter we did not go into. On an effort to keep the subject matter honed, it must be limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the examination-in-chief, I referred to that. It was said that before the conflict the relationships were good, and I am talking about an event before the conflict that speaks to the opposite, and so I believe that I am staying within the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, continue. You may continue with your question, but do not be long. Keep it as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very short indeed. So is it true that when there was this conflict over this wood at the checkpoint that there were two groups of Muslims and Croats who drew guns and there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no shooting, just there was an argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: With the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. R, again I have to show you this time your statement you gave to the investigators, when you say: "About 20 or 30 of us, that is Muslims, came to help the guards. The Croats told us to lower the Bosnian flag ."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody took any positions, they just came to talk. They first took down their own flags and then they came to take down our own flags.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that what you said to the investigators for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you repeat this to me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: "After this problem arose, about 20 or 30 of us came to help the guards. The Croats were telling us to take down the Bosnian flag. Both sides took up the position for fighting."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that that is how I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that is wrong too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I think that we have already settled this problem. The fact that the witness is making contradictions may be, I understand, a source of questions for you, but the Tribunal is not led astray by that. What is important is to know what the witness has to say today. I do not have the statement. You are emphasising certain things, you are emphasising the contradictions, which is your right, but what is of interest to the judges, and I am asking the witness to look at us when he speaks, is we want to know what he has to say today. You may underscore the contradiction, but we are not going to carry out an investigation into it. Do not investigate into contradictions. There will always be contradictions in the statements. Even if it is only because this was a statement taken what year -- can you tell me what date it was, before the investigators from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 1995, that is two years ago. Ask the question if you like, so we hear what his answer is today when he is in a better mental frame, ask him a question and he will answer the judges. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am just trying to refresh the witness's memory by these quotes, but personally I think that it is not completely without significance with respect to the credibility of the witness, whether he changes his statements and views over the course of the years. But we can move on to another area now. These soldiers who came to the SPS factory, the military factory, were they from Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many of them did arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Again, let me remind you what you stated to the investigators. You said that they came in two Dites, military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is when they arrived in Veceriska, into the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Then two military vehicles brought the soldiers from Herzegovina and they came to the SPS military factory. So you said that these soldiers arrived in the Slobodan Princip Selo factory. Did I remember well that you told the Prosecutor that these soldiers brought an anti-aircraft gun and you identified this anti-aircraft gun on these photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They drove it through the village and that is precisely the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that is precisely the one. Let me quote to you again, you told the investigators that these soldiers brought with them an anti-aircraft gun with three barrels. Here we have an anti-aircraft gun with one barrel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you look closer at the picture, they are all in the same line so you cannot see it from the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the eve of the attack of the 16th April, were there tensions in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No tensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you noticed that the Croats were evacuating the civilians, was that any signal for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because we did not expect this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where were your wife and children that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife and children were in Vitez, because I was from Vitez -- she was from Vitez and so my mother-in-law was watching the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, a day or two before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did Muslims in Donje Veceriska have any guards on the eve of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe, but I do not know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us move to the event when the explosion happened, you were running with a child and a piece of concrete hit you in the chest. You saw some soldiers. Did you recognise anyone? If you did, can you tell the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised Milko Franjic, I recognised Dragan Sapina, and I also recognised Vlado Franjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised Mosunj, but he was painted, he was Bokso's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you recognise Vlado Drmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Slavko Franjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me counsel, I am not getting the translation as to what his answer is. I am not getting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am getting it, your Honour, I think we are on the same channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think we should ask the translators if they are getting it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is a bit fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is the same channel, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, what has happened is it is a bit fast and they are going on top of one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I just suggest that they say "question" and "answer", because sometimes we think it is the same person speaking in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So among the present, were there Vlado Drmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Slavko Franjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Anto Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Slavko Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Drmic Zvonko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were these all your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that at one point you decided to run.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief to the Prosecutor, that is what you said. I would like to remind you again in the statement you gave to the state security service, you said as follows, that you saw these people: "They let us pass, and we ran towards the Muslim hamlet of Brdo." In other words, did you flee from them or did they let you go and run away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I started running from Dzemo Haskic's house, that I went to the road and ran there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you came to them, they let you pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they said to put my arms up behind my head and then after that, I went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, you said that you encountered 50 soldiers with patches, HVO, HV and U.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am going to read back to you what you said to the state security in Zenica: "We came to the road by the house where there were about 30 uniformed people, members of the HVO. Some of them had Us on the hats and the chequer board within the U. They let us go through." In other words, you do not mention HV, just HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were also the HV among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that Elvedina Haskic, your cousin, called you and said that her father was hit in the explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How was he injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see. I only saw that he was all bloodied, from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did she tell you how her father was hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am going to read you back what you said to the investigators. What you said to the investigators of the state security service --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, which state security? What do you call "state security"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of the Bosnian government. This is the Muslim state security in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When (redacted), pointed a rifle at you, in the examination-in-chief you told the Prosecutor you did not know what he had told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did not understand that well and I went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am going to remind you what you said to the investigators of the Prosecutor and if it refreshes your memory, please confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. When he reads from the particular document, first I would ask him to read it accurately. The second, more importantly, if he could not use any name to identify the witness as counsel just did. We put the redaction in on that, but however, if we are going to read another quote, it does have a particular identifying feature in there. It is an extremely small village and with nicknames it is easy to identify someone. I ask counsel to be cautious in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you rather have a private session? We are almost at our break. Would you prefer that we work in a private session? Perhaps that would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We could, yes we could for this one sentence, even though I would like to point out that we needed to redact a portion of the examination-in-chief where the identifying features also appeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I say this to Witness R, if something comes out, it is immediately indicated by the Registrar and I ask the technical services to erase them from the transcript. All right. Do you want to ask your last question now and then we will take a break? But be careful when you name names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the person who pointed the rifle at you, did he say, "fuck Gospa, you do not kill Coso", and then he turned around and went away. If you would like, we can make a break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see that there is that the Prosecutor wishes to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am asking a question, Mr. President, were we in private session with that particular question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, without emphasising that particular point, that is exactly my point, the question counsel just asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will redact that statement, at least the names, so the names do not appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I do not see any other solution, but I am very sensitive to these needs for protecting the witnesses, as are my colleagues. I ask Defence counsel to be particularly careful and if necessary, do not hesitate to ask for a private session. Another comment, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think if counsel is addressing a particular portion of the statement he should indicate ahead of time exactly the line and page of the document that he is going to ask from, I will be sensitive to exactly where he is going to ask a potentially damaging question when it comes to this witness's identity. When we go from page to page, it is difficult for me to object ahead of time concerning identifying information, so I would ask counsel to be cautious of that and just indicate page to page where he is going.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We can do that, your Honour, but my colleague is working from the original signed Croatian Bosnian language version. If that will help our colleague, we will give him that, but I doubt it will help him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is not a question about the document, what the Prosecutor is saying is that when Mr. Nobilo quotes a passage from the document, that he is even approximately that it is around the middle of page 3, that can be done. All right, I think everybody needs a break and we will start again at 11.40. (11.20 am) (A short break) (11.40 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now continue. Are you relaxed enough to continue, Witness R?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Witness R, is it true that you reached Meho Haskic's summer kitchen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the summer kitchen of Mahmut Haskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And among the men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember who were there among the men. Nevza's husband was there and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me read you your statement to the investigator --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are in public now, Mr. Nobilo, I am just reminding you. This is a public hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, there will be no more problems. I will take care, do not worry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What are you trying to get to, Mr. Nobilo? It is the same question I asked the Prosecution. What is the objective of this long series of questions you are asking on a document in Serbo-Croat that was given before the security services? You do know, and we have already said this at the beginning of the trial, that we are not investigating investigations. We are not super investigators, if you like. The judges are responsible to judge crime against humanity, for which the General has been accused. You are trying to shake the credibility of this witness, but we have to get to the essential. What is the objective of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I shall try and explain. Our primary goal is not to impeach this witness, that is our secondary goal. It follows automatically. But my next series of questions, I can say quite frankly that we are trying to prove that this witness has left out two and a half days of struggle between the BiH army and the HVO. This witness said that the whole village was burnt down, but only 10 per cent of the houses were burnt down during the fighting, and a limited number of people, so there was no violence against civilians and civilian structures in the sense of destruction of those buildings, but there were combat operations in that village, and this witness, in his previous statement, said those things, but now in the direct examination he has omitted all that. Whether he did so on purpose or unintentionally, that is something we are trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Continue then, but get to the essentials. I would like things to be very clear, out of courtesy to witnesses who have a great deal of suffering. Therefore say that you are simply questioning the credibility of the witness. Now go directly to the question and do not go through round about ways which are wasting a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only thing I would ask is if counsel would refer to the document he is reading from and the page of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: He has not begun yet. Let him begin at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, next to the summer kitchen of the Haskic, was the front-line between the HVO and the Territorial Defence right there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a classical front-line. They had to defend their very lives, their children, because the same thing would have happened to us had it not been for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore next to the Haskic summer kitchen was some kind of armed resistance by the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would have suffered the same fate had it not been for this. All the civilians would have been killed, so I cannot agree with you that only 10 per cent of the houses were burned down. There is a picture, there are many more houses were burned down, virtually all the Muslim houses were burnt and eight civilians were killed, and you are disputing that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We will come back to that later. Can you answer my question. Was any resistance put up, armed resistance put up next to the summer kitchen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in that kitchen and I do not know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am now reading from the Croatian statement, statement in Croatian, on page 5: "Next to the kitchen, the front-line was established between the HVO and the Territorial Defence" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If it is the document that we were given by the Registrar, I only have a document which ends on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am reading from the statement made to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, which has not been admitted into evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So I am quoting: "Next to the kitchen, a front-line had been established between the HVO and the Territorial Defence. Since we were so close to the front-line, we knew that we could not stay in the kitchen." Is this what you told the investigators of the Prosecution of The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could not resist the fierce fire of the HVO against the kitchen, so we had to abandon it and run to another house that had a basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question; did you say this to the investigators or did you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I cannot agree with what you are doing, Mr. Nobilo. Mr. Kehoe, I do not need you to say anything. You have already asked this question three times, having to do with the front-line near the kitchen. The witness has already answered you, you have to make do with the answer and move to another question. We are not going to spend this entire cross-examination on the front-line. You have said what your objections are, that there was combat there and this is something which the witness did not mention in his statement. You have the right to bring this out, but we can stop talking now about the front-line and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I shall proceed, but this front-line moved and the fighting went on for two days after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have noted it, the Tribunal knows this, it is in the transcript, there are documents, there is evidence, there is everything. In our deliberations, we will have thousands and thousands of documents. Trust the judges and move to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. So, when you left the kitchen, summer kitchen, did you reach Elvedin Haskic's house and his two brothers, Mahmut and Samija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the summer kitchen belonged to Mahmut Haskic, when we reached this other house, owned by Cazim Haskic, we went into the basement where there was water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was any armed resistance put up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember, because I was in the cellar and I was out of my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will read again from what you told the investigators on page 3 in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: To the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, the record is page 3 in the middle. Perhaps I shall try and read it in English: "... and his two brothers Mahmut and Samija and two cousins, Mirso and Menso, who were resisting the attack trying to protect us. We stayed there about three hours resisting the shelling and grenades." Did you say that and is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember very well whether that was what I said, but I was in the basement at the time and there were many women and children and people were crying and screaming and we were under very heavy fire, and more than 40 shells fell in and around that house in a hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was Midhat Haskic with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many people, I cannot recall exactly who.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about Midhat Haskic? Has he died in the meantime, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he died after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that you then went to Zlotrg, to Besa Zlotrg's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all left, we had to go, but we waited for nightfall to cross over to Brdo, not only to his house, everybody was terribly upset, exhausted, and in the evening, we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So can we conclude that you spent the 16th in these locations that we have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 17th or the night between the 16th and 17th, is it true that you moved to Brdo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me again read from the statement you made, it is also on page 3, towards the end of the page, to The Hague investigators, and you said: "The villagers in Brdo put up a defence line, though they did not have much weapons. The line was kept up that night, the next day and the following night. In the morning on the 18th April, UNPROFOR arrived."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no line , it was no front-line. There was a lull at the time, so we spent the whole day there and then in the evening, about 2.00 or 3.00, the night between the 17th and 18th , we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did the HVO enter the village on the 16th, your part of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more than half the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did it manage to enter the second half?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 18th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore the HVO entered the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We watched all that in front of the UNPROFOR garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the HVO entered on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They entered before, but when we saw the houses on fire, we knew that the HVO had entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you join the struggle at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me read again, only I have to find the place in the English version. It is in the second statement on page 4: "At one point in time, I had to assist the TO when one of the members was wounded. The wounded member was a refugee from Karaule." Did you tell the investigators that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And in your second statement to the investigators on page 4, you said, "I took a rifle".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never took a rifle, because in this general chaos, I was not even aware where I was, never mind capable of doing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me whether the UNPROFOR came throughout the conflict to evacuate the wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would pass by and we were happy to see them, hoping they would save us. However, they only picked up those who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many Muslims did you have under arms there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You told The Hague investigators, "40 to 50 rifles".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Here again from your second statement on page 4, it says: "We only had 40 or 50 rifles."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not, nothing like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to intervene here. You are showing the contradictions that the witness has made and you are entitled to do so, but what counts for the judges in the end is the reality of the testimony as it is presented today. Witness R, I know it is a bit complicated, but this is the judge now asking you the question, and through me my colleagues as well. There is a statement which you made, we can understand that it is important for the Defence, you are under oath. Were there 40 or 50 rifles or none at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not saying that there were no rifles, but I did not say that there were 45 to 50, because in view of all that had happened to me, I did not count. I did not know how many men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But there were rifles, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As Bosnia-Herzegovina was attacked by the Serbian Montenegrin aggressor, the people who were on the front-lines near Turbe or wherever they were, that does not matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do not apologise, we are not here in order to ask you for justification. Just a specific point about which we are asking questions, that there were rifles. That was all I was asking, there were rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were, but not the number mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. That is fine. Thank you very much, Witness R. Continue, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the withdrawal on the third day or at dawn of the third day, is it true what you said to the investigators of the Prosecution: "The Territorial Defence was short of ammunition and that is why the civilians had to withdraw about 1.00 or 2.00 am, escorted by an UNPROFOR vehicle. Then the TO members retreated because we were left without any ammunition. All members of the TO were inhabitants of the village. We went through the SPS factory compound and we were shot at by the HVO. The members of the Territorial Defence went on to the village of Grbavica".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me counsel, which statement are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, I am waiting for the end of the interpretation. Mr. Kehoe, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am asking counsel which statement he is reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Page 4 of the statement dated 16th February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So I am asking whether you retreated when you ran out of ammunition on the third day and is it true that the TO unit went to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know anything about the ammunition or whatever. I really do not know, because I was not in good shape, I just know that we reached the UNPROFOR, that they helped us, gave us some coffee and some tea, so I do not know where other people went to. The world surely knows where we were and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But did you say this, that the TO went to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I did, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see the TO unit heading towards Grbavica when you headed for the UNPROFOR echelon. You told the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There is a mistake, because my answer appears as the question. Now we have the answer. Thank you. When you were heading towards the UNPROFOR echelon and you were shot at from the factory, was there any light, or was it dark and could you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the column was very large, one could see the firing coming from the gates of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was anyone killed at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know in which direction the fire was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether they were shooting at us or not, I know that people were screaming, but no one was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you do not know where the fire was directed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot know, because it was night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you follow UN vehicles going to the echelon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were guards around the battalion. At one point, they probably saw this large group of people coming, so they switched on the lights. We shouted they should switch them off and that is how we reached the echelon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you were evacuated from the echelon to Zenica by the UN and the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did they evacuate together with your group civilians from another village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from Stari Vitez, because after the explosion, there were many wounded, and also some people from Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were any people from Gacice evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly whether any people from Gacice were evacuated, but I do not believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your late parents were buried, as you said, in Stari Vitez. Will you tell me whether the other people from your village were buried there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the eight people killed were buried in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Out of the eight people killed, did you personally see any one of those murders and the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw the killing of Meho Haskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you saw him being killed personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him fall to the ground in a pool of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will read again a part of your statement to the investigators, just one sentence, when you said: "When I approached Meho Haskic's house" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am just trying to get a reference from what counsel is reading. If he is reading the Bosnian statement, if he is reading an ICTY statement? I have no indication what he is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, would you make it clear, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am reading the translation of the investigation statement which we received from the Prosecution, the first statement. With your indulgence, maybe I could find the exact position, but I shall try and read it very carefully and correctly: "When we approached the house of Meho Haskic, I saw him lying dead next to his house, riddled with bullets from a machine-gun. I later heard from his daughter that somebody called Cano had killed him." So did you see him being killed or did you hear later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him fall when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So what you told the investigators is not correct, that is that his daughter told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see any other killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During the fighting, did any Croat houses burn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say, I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many houses did you personally observe burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact number. I saw many houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will now read what you told the investigators on pages 4 and 5 of your statement of 16th February 1995: "I saw" -- pages 4 and 5 of the statement made by the witness to The Hague investigators, the second statement, dated 16th February 1995: "While I was in the village, I saw the following houses and stables on fire, Haskic Smajo, Haskic Mujo, Haskic Rahima, Sis Salko, Haskic Ramo, Haskic Kazim, Haskic Nasid, Haskic Fehro, Haskic Zirafeta, Haskic Saban", all Haskics, then, "Ahmet Suljakovic, Muharem Besic, Haskic Redjo, Zlotrg Nerka, Kalco Ferid." Those are the houses and the stables that you saw on fire, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you did not see any others in addition to those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw many houses burning and when I was asked, "could you list the houses that were burned down?", that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that 12 civilians from the UNPROFOR echelon returned to the school, when they left the UNPROFOR echelon, they went back to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not a single civilian went back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: -- with the examination-in-chief, I would like things to go back to the examination-in-chief, please. It does not have a direct connection with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There must always be a connection. Intellectually there can always be relationships made, that is philosophically speaking, but the judge in this case must say that the cross-examination has to remain within the scope of the examination, with a certain degree of manoeuvrability, we are not rigid. This is of no interest at all and I ask you to go to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We do not insist on this question. I am going to read the names of some people of whom we have been informed that they participated in the struggles, so if you know, please say yes, if no, say no. Abdulah Haskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is this involved the subject matter here? Counsel said involved in the struggles. What struggles?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In Donje Veceriska, from 16th to 18th April 1993, on the side of the BiH army against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who participated, nor did I see who participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The central point of the cross-examination is legitimate in this case. He wanted to explain, which is why I wanted to be clear what the principle of the cross-examination here is. It is legitimate for Mr. Nobilo and his other Defence attorney to say whether there was combat or not. This is of some importance to the judges, so the question can be asked and you will exercise your right of re-examination if you do not agree, but the central issue is whether or not there were days which can be part of the conflict which was expressed more differently in your examination. Let the question be asked, if the witness cannot answer he will say so. The question can be asked, continue in light of what the witness answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you name the people who fought in Donje Veceriska from 16th April at dawn until 18th April at dawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot, because I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you learn later whether he participated in the conflict or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are now giving out names and perhaps we have to go back into private session, because this could cause difficulties for the witness. I would like this to be a private session now. Mr. Dubuisson, have that done, please. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Witness R, Defence counsel asked you some questions as to whether Donje Veceriska was on a slight hill just above the defence factory, do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Defence counsel also asked you whether the village of Gacice on the other side of the Defence factory was also on a hill above the defence factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the Muslims in the village of Donje Veceriska or anywhere else ever attack HVO troops or HV troops, or any other troops in the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You told us that you were a member of the TO, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also told counsel a list of names of individuals that you recognised who were from your village, who were Croats who were participating in this attack, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But there were also people that you did not recognise, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many I did not recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, that there were soldiers coming from outside Donje Veceriska, it is something we heard about at great length in the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, please keep your comments for your final argument. This is a question which is part of the right of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were asked a question by Defence counsel about your brother being in another part of the village defending his family, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you hear that other people defended their families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everyone was defending his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were asked questions by Defence counsel about a front-line, do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there a brigade or a division or a corps of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army in Donje Veceriska fighting the Croat troops that were moved through the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course not. Nothing like it. These were just locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you told us that there are no Muslims living in the town today, either, are there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have been making much ado through cross-examination of the discrepancies between the statements that were given by the witness, the statement given in April 1993 by the witness to the Bosnians in Zenica, and the statement given to the investigators of the war crimes Tribunal here in The Hague, given February 16th 1993. I offer both of these items into evidence. Unfortunately I have not had the opportunity to translate them into French, but I offer them into the record at this point, for whatever the last two exhibit numbers are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like all the statements made Defence exhibits and there are not simply these two. My colleague Mr. Nobilo has referred to a number. First, we have an English translation of Defence Exhibit D69, we would offer that. We would also offer a statement to the Tribunal dated 5th February 1994, and we would offer the second statement to the Tribunal investigators, dated February 16th 1995. I have them all here, I will tender them with the court's permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the Defence Exhibit D69, obviously we likewise want to make them Prosecution exhibits. D69, of course, is problematical, because Defence counsel has obviously written on this. What we offer is a clean copy without Defence counsel's notations on it and likewise we offer the English translation that has been provided to Defence counsel. As I noted, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to summarise. The central issue involves knowing whether there was combat on the front-line, whether families were being defended, whether the village was being defended. This, of course, is important both for the Prosecution and Defence. Mr. Kehoe, you are offering all the statements, if I am not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. To the extent that there are discrepancies in any way, shape or form, I suggest we just offer it to the President and your Honours and let the facts fall where they may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
