utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When we left off, Colour Sergeant Parrott, we were talking about you picking the accused up at the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was he alone or was he with a group of people? Could you describe it to the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, normally he would have approximately six to eight bodyguards, heavily armed. He would usually be one of the only people who did not have a weapon visible at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I show you a document that I believe you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Dubuisson, may I hand Exhibit 171 to the witness. Colour Sergeant Parrott, do you recognise Exhibit 171?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The top sheet is a translation of a fax received by headquarters Vitez requesting transport from Kiseljak to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you said headquarters Vitez, from headquarters Vitez, whose headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you read the translation that you received, translation of that letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is headed, "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council. Central Bosnia Ops Command", I am not sure of the next part: "... before Vitez. Number 01-4-163/93, date 11th April 1993. Time, 1100 hours. Defence military secret, highly confidential. A request for providing armoured personnel carriers for transport. Could you please provide two armoured personnel carriers for transport of a HVO delegation and their escort on 12th April 1993, Monday. Place of departure, Kiseljak HVO barracks. Route, Kiseljak Kacuni, Busovaca. Time of departure, 0900. Number of passengers, ten members of the delegation. Having appreciated your understanding in transporting us before, we are expecting a positive answer. We are grateful in advance. Could you inform us about the outcome of our request by 1600 hours on 11th April 1993. In written form or by telephone, 712-902. With respect, Commander Colonel T Blaskic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that written translation, there is a yellow note, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What does that say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Only allow Blaskic and 7 men and int rep to be brought along".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a request of Blaskic to take them from Kiseljak to Busovaca through Kacuni, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know, Colour Sergeant, whether or not this particular request was complied with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know for definite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But similar requests to this were complied with by the British battalion, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, your Honours, I have completed my questioning of this witness and I just would like to offer into evidence the maps that are on the easel, Exhibit 45G, 56G, 50I, 56H, 55A, 75A, 76B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And 170, the photo album.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The photo album, 170, and the series of letters with their translation as 171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to be sure about the numbering of the transport orders. We will now, Sergeant, have the cross-examination, Mr. Hayman is going to cross-examine you. Go ahead, please, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, excuse me, to the extent that there is a confusion with this document, there are actually two translations of the letter, one that was given to Sergeant Parrott and one that was done by the Tribunal. If that is a source of confusion, that is the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I understood that there were translations that were done on site. That is what you are talking about, is it not? That were done by the British battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then you had the translation into French and English which represent the last document. All right, everything is under 170. Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We do not object to the admission of any of the exhibits, but I would like to note for the record that this is the first time we have been provided with Exhibit 171, which is a statement of the accused. Under Rule 66 we are entitled to statements of the accused when they first come into the possession of the Prosecutor. I see here they have had time to produce a French translation, but they apparently did not have time to give this to the Defence when they got it in advance of the testimony. If I am wrong, I apologise, but I do not believe we have seen this before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is a relevant question. According to Rule 66, all information must be communicated to the Defence. It is not exactly a statement, but as a document whose author is the accused, we have to be very careful in the terminology that we use. Is that not right, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely right, Mr. President. However, it is not his statement. There are any number of orders in the possession of the Tribunal signed by the accused. They are not the defendant's statements. Again, had we engaged in reciprocal discovery this problem would have been covered. We have not, through the choice of the Defence counsel. Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour. Excuse me, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, this particular document came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor last week in discussions with Colour Sergeant Parrott. I must be very clear that the position throughout this trial, and never raised by Defence counsel, was that the orders of the defendant were statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hayman. I would like to remind you that we dealt with this issue in the decision of 27th January 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I can refresh the court's recollection, that decision said that a statement is a statement, regardless of who took it, regardless of the form it is in and regardless of whether it is signed or otherwise sworn or adopted. If the court accepts Mr. Kehoe's position, so be it, but the record should be absolutely clear that we made a motion for all statements, the court ruled, and if statements such as this order are not being provided to the Defence, that should be in the record, it should be absolutely clear and our objection is noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We had the opportunity to settle this issue. But unfortunately, my copy is not good. The principle said that in support of 66(A), the Tribunal says that all previous statements of the accused will be given to the -- it is stated that these would come from any other source. The interpretation for 66(A) says that the Trial Chamber cannot make a distinction between the form or forms of these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do not have this statement in the interpretation booth, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Going back to paragraph 37, I think we did that in order to simplify things. We consider that everything that comes from the Prosecution has to be given to the Defence so that he can prepare the Defence. This should be clear, we are wasting time here. I do not think there is any point in this. We could go on and on discussing what does the word "statement" mean, but we settled this on 27th January 1997, when you said that everything that came from the accused has to be given Defence. I think this is in order to keep things fair and part of an adversarial procedure. What do you think about that? We are not going to redo our decision of 27th January, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. President, in Rule 66(B), which is the reciprocal discovery, it says: "The Prosecutor shall on request, subject to sub-rule (C), permit the Defence to inspect any documents in its custody that they are going to use." These are documents in our custody that we intend to use during the trial. That is certainly the subject of a reciprocal discovery issue and not the issue of statements where the particular defendant makes a statement in the media which we have given over, makes a statement to a newspaper or an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have to reargue this. The court ruled, the Prosecutor is making his position absolutely clear in the record. It will speak for itself, for this court, for any appellate proceeding. I suggest we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am grateful for Mr. Hayman's assistance, but I believe quite clearly that the particular documents Defence wants we could have got through the reciprocal discovery procedures, but he chose not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment. (Pause). The Tribunal considers that for the time being, it will keep this in abeyance. For the time being this will be part of the cross-examination and discussed by the Defence, and we will come back to this, but not at the bench, to the decision, in a decision which was rendered by a trial bench which did not include one of the judges who are here now. So for the time being, Mr. Hayman, you can discuss the document if you desire but if you do not so desire that, of course, is your right. If I understood you correctly, you wish to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are prepared to proceed with cross-examination, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colour Sergeant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have a few questions but not too many. Can you help us fix approximately when on the morning of 16th April 1993 you arrived in the Vitez town area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was some time shortly after 0900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You had been on alert for a couple of hours before then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would say a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you with Lieutenant Dooley all day on 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the total number of HVO soldiers you saw in the Vitez, Stari Vitez area on 16th April that morning, 1993, was around two dozen, approximately two dozen soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact number would be extremely difficult. I would say that that would be on the low side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would three dozen be on the high side, or can you say with any more specificity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not particularly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have indicated on I believe the exhibit that is currently on display, Exhibit 45G, that you saw a certain number of HVO soldiers moving house to house on the morning of 16th April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the number of those soldiers around six?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, around the houses visible to us, I would say that was approximate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many houses did you see them move through while you were observing those six or so soldiers on the morning of April 16th 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw them move from a position concealed to us through to the rear of the houses where they were directly in front of the armoured vehicle, so that would be through the rear garden of one house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they provide each other cover with their weapons while they moved, or were you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, they tended to move into fire positions in amongst the outbuildings and the garden walls and fences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by "fire positions"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be a position taken up to either fire a weapon from, or alternatively to get into, a position which would afford some sort of cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you said that these six soldiers appeared organised, do you mean in substance that they were moving in a way in which their relationship with each other was organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Had you seen by contrast other soldiers, for example at checkpoints, who had seemed pretty disorganised during your tour in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any of these six soldiers fire any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see them light any houses on fire with any instruments, fuel or anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You describe seeing an used or discarded RPG 16 in the street. If that weapon were fired into a house, and it detonated, would it be capable of setting the house on fire, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether that type of weapon, an RPG, is something that would commonly be used during fighting in built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, the six male Muslims that you saw at the end of the cul-de-sac, do you recall those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were they in mixed uniform, that is partial uniform, partial civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my recollection, I believe only a portion of those six had any type of uniform at all. In that way, it would be mixed uniform as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was a mixed uniform, in your view, a customary form of dress for BiH soldiers in this area at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some areas, mixed uniform was customary for most of the forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of these six men whom you saw, I take it one or more had shotguns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did one or more have AK 47s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You describe seeing another man with some type of small arms weapon who was in a garden with a cow, do you recall that individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see that individual making a motion which appeared to be the motion of throwing a hand grenade in the direction of the six HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you locked down in your Warrior at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Before the six HVO soldiers withdrew, did you see some additional Muslim men arrive in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if this refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe, I will provide you with the page. It is page 5 of the statement to the Tribunal investigators, dated 27th April 1995. In discussing this situation, the statement states: "Shortly after some time, some more Muslim men arrived, but I would not describe them as soldiers or a unit, but just a male presence from the town in various remnants of uniform. The families in the house ran from the building in the direction of Stari Vitez. It now appeared that the Muslim men were prepared to defend the houses in their vicinity." Does that refresh your recollection as to whether some additional Muslim men in mixed uniform arrived at the scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe if that was in my statement then that would have been a recollection at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it it is not a recollection you have today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at present, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In any event, after a passage of some time, did the six HVO soldiers withdraw from the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they do so with no exchange of fire, with the six Muslim males you have described at the end of the cul-de-sac or any other persons in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No firing was seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described later on that morning you saw a house on fire below the stadium, that is if you are looking at one of these exhibits, on the photograph below the stadium, away from Vitez town, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that one house on fire or more than one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only have a definite recollection of one house which was burning particularly fiercely. However, there may have been others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Later in the day, you went on the Vitez-Busovaca road and helped to collect bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The five bodies that were collected at, I believe, point 5 on one of the maps, did they all have the same wound, or did they have different types of wounds, insofar as you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not personally responsible for putting those people in the ambulance, but from what was told to me afterwards, they all had bullet wounds; however, some were in different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They were not all shot in the head in the same way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The photos that are, I believe the first two photos in Exhibit 170, which I am holding up, do you know, are these persons who were two of the five that were picked up on that afternoon, or are they other individuals, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no definite information whether they were the first lot or the second lot that we actually picked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You cannot tell or you do not remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell from those photographs which of those two it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let us turn, if we may, to 17th April 1993, your visit to Donje Veceriska. You stated on the way up, and perhaps the usher could assist, your Honour, and we could have Exhibit 55A before us, should it prove useful to the witness. You stated on the drive up to Donje Veceriska you encountered some 20 or more civilians by the road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there some BiH army or BiH militia with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there may have been, I think, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were they in a mixed dress or how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no definite recollection of their exact dress.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe if they were described as militia they may well have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think if I may trouble you, if you could join me, and I invite my counsel from across the bar, as it would be of assistance to look at Exhibit 55A during the next several questions I have. You indicated the area on Exhibit 55A which I believe you circled in red as including the area in which you saw a number of HVO soldiers, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tell me, those HVO soldiers, were they standing in an open field, were they behind a structure, in a ravine? Can you describe the type of location that they were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main street has houses either side, but near the junction is fairly open. The soldiers were just around the main street and the main concentration being around the junction area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say "the junction", are you talking about the area circled in green?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, near there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where did you first see any males of fighting age, if you will, whom you believe to be of the Muslim -- part of the Muslim community in Donje Veceriska. Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from the people we met on the way up there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Once you got up into the village proper, where did you first see any Muslim males of fighting age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe where I marked number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could you point that out again, if you do not mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around this area here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The top of the loop as you drove round your circle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is actually at the top of the loop.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you are saying you did not see any evidence of the Muslim community, if you will, down around the road which is the upper half of the red circle on this Exhibit 55A; but above the road from the red circle, did you see any evidence of the Muslim community or any Muslim fighting-aged men in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you got around to, on the photograph, the top of the circle or loop and as you have described it being in the lower ground, you did encounter some Muslim men of fighting age, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many did you find there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there were only possibly two men that you would refer to as fighting age.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did any of them have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there was a civilian rifle of some sort, and I think a shotgun, I am not exactly sure. I think you can see weapons on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There is a weapon that you can see in the corner of Exhibit 170, I believe it is 170/4, the photograph of the -- if you could step forward and take my copy, if you do not have my copy. This is the photograph of the -- perhaps another copy could be placed on the ELMO while the witness is looking at it, of a Warrior in a narrow lane. If you look to the left of the Warrior, do you see a man standing with a firearm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks very much like a shotgun from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the photograph on the ELMO could be moved a little to the right so that this individual is in view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I heard the interpretation as "revolver", is that correct? Yes, I think that is my confusion. I do not know about military strategy, but I think there is a difference between a revolver and a rifle. I do not know if it is for war or for hunting, but it is certainly not a revolver. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This gun was neither a revolver -- it was not a revolver, correct, the weapon that you spotted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not a revolver, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is some type of a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But from the photograph you cannot discern --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object, your Honour. He said it was a shotgun.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what you asked me before, I would say it was a shotgun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There was a translation problem. I was not trying to confuse the witness, just trying to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, it was an interpretative problem, but the interpreters did not have the photograph in front of them. I am sure that it is a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there any HVO soldiers in this part of the village where you encountered these men, that is at the upper part of the photograph which is Exhibit 55A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were none around where I have marked number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How long did you spend in Donje Veceriska on this day, 17th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact time is not confirmed, however I would say from start to finish possibly an hour and a half, two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you have an interpreter with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection of having an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you gain any information from the persons on the ground as to what was going on, what the situation was, in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, in the village they were more concerned about trying to get someone evacuated from the village. I have no recollection of any definite details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This wounded man you describe, he was, I take it, at the top of the loop, at the upper portion of the photograph which is 55A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were only told about him, we did not actually see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You did not know where he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While you were there, did you see any HVO soldiers firing their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you evacuate any wounded from Donje Veceriska on that trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you send someone else to pick up some wounded later or make other arrangements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was reported when we got back to Vitez. The further action is unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, you may have a seat. Perhaps Exhibit 170 has been provided to you -- perhaps not all of it. Perhaps Exhibit 170/4, which is the picture of the fire, could be provided to the witness and placed on the ELMO. Thank you. Colour Sergeant, this photo, can you tell us what kind of structure is burning in this photo? Were you able to tell at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It appeared that the main structure of the building had actually burnt and the thing that was on fire there was the log pile to the side of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The main structure, do you know, was it a house or a summer kitchen or a stable, or could you tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no real indication as to what it was, it was in too bad a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there any other houses burning in the vicinity -- or stables burning in the vicinity of this fire while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection of any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of any other burning structures anywhere else in Donje Veceriska while you were visiting it on 17th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that any of them were actually on fire at that stage. However, I cannot confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described picking up Colonel Blaskic in Kiseljak on one occasion and transporting him to Busovaca, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it you did that once, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have only a definite recollection of one occasion. However, it was done several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: By others, but not you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly myself as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But you have a distinct recollection of one trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On that one trip, were you told the purpose of the transportation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The occasion that you transported Colonel Blaskic from Kiseljak to Busovaca, at the time, was the weather extremely cold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know the reason you were being asked to transport him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I object. This question was just asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will rephrase, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am referring to not the purpose of his travel but why he needed UN protection to travel from Kiseljak to Busovaca. Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he felt that he needed a protected journey on that particular road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that because the BiH army held a stretch of the road from Busovaca to Kiseljak, or were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact territorial positions were not known to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How did you describe the location where you picked up Colonel Blaskic in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is basically known as the HVO barracks in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On your excursions in Vitez on 16th April 1993, did you see any soldiers wearing HV patches or insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By HV, does that include HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, I am referring to HV, as in the army of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only insignia that was definitely evident was red and white chessboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about on the road on 16th April when you were making various trips on the road, the Busovaca-Vitez road; did you see any HV insignia or patches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, only identifiable by red and white chessboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How about in Donje Veceriska on 17th April 1993? Did you see any HV patches or insignia among any of the soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again same answer, red and white chessboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Only HVO patches, not HV patches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection of specifically seeing any HV patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. You were asked a question by Defence counsel concerning the organisation of the soldiers in Stari Vitez on the morning of the 16th, do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He asked you whether or not you believed that they were organised because they appeared to be operating together, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They had other items on their uniforms that indicated that they were working together, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had -- all of the soldiers in that particular group had a piece of ribbon tied around their epaulette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if soldiers with the same type of ribbon had the same colour on their epaulette and other soldiers in other places in the Lasva Valley had a similar type of demarcation, would it indicate to you as a soldier that those soldiers in those locations were working together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Defence counsel asked you a question about the events when you were in the cul-de-sac in, around Stari Vitez. Prior to that attack, had the civilians in that area been evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did that indicate to you as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That at that time they were trapped where they were and there was nowhere really for them to go at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it indicate to you, Colour Sergeant, that they had been taken by surprise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you observe, after the HVO soldiers withdrew, a man crying on a stoop near these burning houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same man who had the cow on a rope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Counsel asked you a question as to whether or not these HVO soldiers withdrew from the area. Did they withdraw from the area before or after your particular company had made a decision to fire on them if they attacked the civilians and trained your turret towards them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did they withdraw after you had turned the barrel of your turret towards them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was around that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your experience in Bosnia, was it common for the violence to stop when an UNPROFOR vehicle came into the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you observe that on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the questions asked by Defence counsel about Donje Veceriska. The Muslims that you saw in the village, and I believe we have it designated as number 5 on the map, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted what you believe were two individuals of fighting age, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have only recollection of approximately two, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there women and children and old people as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You have been a British soldier, an infantry soldier for almost 15 years, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 14 years, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you take shotguns into battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they are not effective for conventional warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you do not consider this to be a weapon that can counter a conventional weapon that a soldier would have, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, you were there for two hours, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see individuals firing back and forth after you entered the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we heard small arms fire; however, we did not see where it was coming from or to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did that surprise you, that the HVO soldiers were not firing when you got into the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was as you stated before, it was quite a common thing to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why? Was it because they did not want you to see what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you conclude as a soldier, Colour Sergeant Parrott? Did you conclude they did not want to let the UN know what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In addition to the fire that they were not putting out, there was a dead body near that location as well, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did any of these soldiers who were not hiding from any gunfire go over and attempt to retrieve this dead body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did that indicate to you as a soldier, Sergeant Parrott?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we are going to go into opinions, I insist that I be granted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I quite agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: -- recross-examination to test these opinions, and I have some opinions I would like to elicit from this witness. The door has been opened wide and that is my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the objection of Mr. Hayman is well-founded and for the moment, I think you must limit yourself, Mr. Kehoe, to questions which are in line with the cross-examination. You have finished, Mr. Kehoe, you have any more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn to my colleagues now. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Sergeant Parrott. You have depicted all the tragic scenes you have been through, which are certainly not customary scenes. Did your regiment raise the matter to the headquarters of the HVO or ask for an explanation, or was it not customary to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what the high command's position was on this. However, I do know that at various stages during our tour attempts were made by Colonel Stewart and the UN to hold talks of one sort or another between the various factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So let us say the headquarters were informed about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which headquarters, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of them being informed or otherwise, but I would imagine that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sergeant, thank you very much for your testimony. There are no further questions, which means that we have completed this testimony. We wish to thank you for your services, and your unit. The usher is going to accompany the witness out. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Harmon? Can we have the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. It will be Ms Paterson, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: No, your Honour, this is not a protected witness. This is another British military officer. Would you like me to give my summary first, before we call the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please, your summary and your objectives.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The next witness is Major Roy Hunter, who was a British military officer serving with the Prince of Wales's own regiment in Yorkshire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A bit more slowly please, for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Major Hunter was assigned to the British battalion in the area of Vitez in May 1993 and served in that area for several months. He will be describing basically three incidents that he participated in or observed. He will be speaking about an incident on 19th May 1993, during which he was awakened by gunfire and saw some Muslim houses across the street that were burning and he will briefly describe some actions that he took in regard to those houses. Then he will discuss a meeting that he attended on 20th May 1993 at the Hotel Vitez, where he met with three leaders of the Croatian Community, leaders of the town of Vitez. He will discuss in some detail that meeting, and the people that he spoke with. Then finally, he will discuss another incident on 20th May in the afternoon, when he also went to the village of Donje Veceriska, and where on 20th May 1993, almost a month after the village was originally attacked, he again observed Muslim houses in the village being burned and had an encounter with some HVO soldiers in that village on that day. That will be basically the substance of his testimony. It is the Prosecution's contention that this testimony will go toward proving count 1 of the indictment, which is the persecution count, specifically paragraph 6.1, attacks on cities, towns and villages, and paragraph 6.6 and 6.7, the forcible transfer of civilians. In addition, he will speak about evidence that goes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, 6.1 and?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: His testimony will also go toward proving counts 11 to 13, destruction and plunder of property, specifically in the village of Donje Veceriska, and he will speak briefly about some incidents related to the village of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your summary, which has been very useful. Mr. Registrar, can we ask the usher to bring the Major in so we can hear him for about a quarter of an hour before we adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just ask Mr. Dubuisson if he could give me the numbers of the premarked exhibits I provided for him earlier? I have not been given the numbers of those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, for the large photograph, aerial photograph, it is Exhibit 172. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Major?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are going to tell the Trial Chamber your name, surname and your rank. Your rank first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major Roy Hunter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please read your solemn declaration while standing. MAJOR ROY HUNTER (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. You may be seated now. You have been called by the Prosecutor within the framework of the trial against General Blaskic. The Prosecution has given us a summary, quite a detailed summary of the three types of incidents that you will be discussing, one on the 19th and two on the 20th, one of which was a meeting with Croatian leaders. After that, the Prosecution will have some questions to put to you, or maybe even in the course of your statement, to clarify the data that go in support of the counts contained in the indictment. Ms. Paterson, you may now begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Major Hunter, just a couple of things before we begin. First of all, as I explained to you before, since we both speak English we need to speak slowly and put some pauses between our questions and answers so the interpreters can keep up, and the judges would prefer as much as possible that you address them when you answer the questions. Major Hunter, did you join the British military in 1978?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Are you currently serving in the Prince of Wales's own regiment of Yorkshire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Are you currently assigned to the Defence School of Languages and are studying Russian at that school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did you go to the former Yugoslavia in the course of your military duties for the first time on a one week reconnaissance to Vitez at the end of February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of February for just one week.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did you return again to Bosnia on 28th April 1993, specifically again to the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: On 11th May 1993, did your regiment, the Prince of Wales's own regiment, assume responsibility from the previous regiment, which was the Cheshire Regiment, in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Major Hunter, would you very briefly just describe for the judges your responsibility and your position when you were serving in Bosnia in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I was a company commander, so I was in command of about 100 or 120 soldiers and about 20 armoured vehicles. So in terms of the British forces in the camp at Stari Bila, it was about 50 per cent of the forces in that location. My company was A Company, the other troops there were from C Company and B Company was down at Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, Major Hunter. You stated that you arrived in Vitez about the end of April 1993. I am going to ask you to discuss some things that happened on 19th May 1993, so would that be fair to say that those events occurred only two or three weeks after you arrived in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It was just at the end of the first week of us being in the theatre, having taken over from the Cheshires.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Major Hunter, I am going to ask you to describe an incident that occurred on 19th May 1993, but before you begin I need to introduce a couple of exhibits that I would like you to refer to during your testimony. First of all, your Honour, we have prepared an enlargement of an aerial photo, but I am told by my colleagues that the large photo from which this is taken has not yet been introduced into evidence, so I need to first move that into evidence. That would be the large original which I believe is placed on the easel, is that correct, Mr. Dubuisson? That is Exhibit 172.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I believe this photograph shows the area of Stari Bila and the British base that was located in that area, the village of Grbavica and some of the villages just outside of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: At this time, could the exhibit, which I guess would be number 173, which is the enlargement taken from that Exhibit 172, could that be placed on the ELMO for the witness? Major Hunter, before you came into court, did you have an opportunity to see this diagram and to prepare it with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Together did we place these numbers and circles on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did you also have an opportunity to examine the legend at the bottom of the diagram and determine whether or not that is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is all correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Major Hunter, if you would describe briefly for the judges what occurred on the morning of 19th May 1993 when you were at your base just outside Vitez. If you would please refer to the diagram while you describe the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. At about 5.00 in the morning, I was still in bed, and this was the accommodation that I was using at that time (indicates). Fourteen British officers were in that house. I was woken by the sound of gunfire, automatic fire. I think maybe 20 or 30 rounds were fired. The noise came from across the road. I looked across to what was happening, I could see that one or two houses were already burning across the road. These were houses occupied at the time by some Muslim families, but the rest of the village down here (indicates) was entirely Croatian by this time, so this was just the very few Muslim houses which remained on that side of the road. The houses around here were also occupied by Muslim families, and there were some Croatian families in these houses here (indicates). What had happened was that the HVO had occupied those houses, and the members of the families, four or five families, had been evicted from the houses and had come across the road and sought refuge amongst the Muslim families around the house where I was staying. One man had been killed on that side, a Mr. Subasic. He was about 60 years old, he was the father of a man I knew that I had been dealing with, called Munib Subasic. But everybody else had been just evicted from the houses and those houses were now alight. This meant that the HVO were able to occupy these houses and create a new front-line, which gave them a good field of fire across the bridge and across the road, because on the far side, on the high ground, on the Grbavica feature, were the front-lines of the ABiH, who occupied houses along the ridge line. So this operation gave the HVO the ability to fire better across the bridge, so it was quite an important bridge which they wanted to control. At that time they were unable to, in fact they were unable to gain total control of this area until September, the first week of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: What happened in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In September 1993, on I think 6th or 7th September, there was quite a large scale HVO assault, using artillery and mortars, and infantry, which secured the whole of the hill feature, Grbavica. After that, the entire village of Grbavica was burnt, by which time there were very few people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sorry, we are talking about 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1993. Did I say the wrong year? 1993, September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, you said it well. 1993, that was several months afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What happened then at about 7.00 in the morning, I took two armoured vehicles across the road to investigate what was going on. There was very little activity by this stage, it was a very quick attack, it probably only took five or ten minutes, so there was nothing really to do on the ground at that time. I simply patrolled past the houses and into the rest of Stari Bila. Meanwhile, a colleague of mine was able to recover the body of Mr. Subasic, and that body was taken to the mosque in Grbavica, which is about 500 metres in this direction for burial. Essentially, that is what happened on the morning of 19th May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps, Ms Paterson, I do not know what your view is, but it is 5.45, perhaps you would prefer to make a clarification regarding this particular incident, in view of the fact that we are going to break very soon and resume tomorrow, or do you prefer to leave it until tomorrow. If it is a point of clarification, maybe we could do it right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I just want to very briefly clarify the numbers and the points on the diagram and then it would be an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I agree then, please go on. Very well, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Major Hunter, you did an excellent job of using the diagram, but you did not describe the numbers as you were pointing to locations. Can I just clarify? The area on the diagram marked number 1, that was where you were having your accommodation, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the house I lived in until September. In September we had to move out, because it had been damaged by mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Number 2 on the diagram is the area where you saw the burning houses, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were not completely burnt. There were fires inside the rooms but the roofs did not collapse.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Number 3 is a series of houses that for some time had been inhabited by Croats, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this time, the houses were not inhabited by families, they were occupied by HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: The line that is marked there with a 3A, would that basically be what you described as the Croat HVO front-line at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they already had positions in these houses and by removing the Muslim families from the houses at number 2, they were able to get a proper complete line all the way up to the river line. They had trenches in the gardens of the houses at number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, and then number 4 would be the area where at that time there were still some Muslim residents residing, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in these houses, these houses were already empty and burnt with no roofs on, but the rest of the village of Grbavica, which is behind number 4, was still occupied by Muslim families.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, and then the line drawn and marked with number 4A, would that basically represent what was at that time the Muslim front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the BiH soldiers were in all of the buildings along here and also in the building here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Hunter. Mr. President, this time I was going to move on to the next incident, so this would be an appropriate time to break, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to interrupt and we will resume tomorrow, but at 10.15. (5.45 pm)

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until 10.15 am the following day)
